title: ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name
description: “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” is a documentary about one of the greatest singers in the history of pop music, but it’s also a stunning medi
body:
“Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” is a documentary about one of the greatest singers in the history of pop music, but it’s also a stunning meditation on the issue of identity in pop. Darlene Love recorded her most defining songs in the early ’60s, when she was part of the Phil Spector hit factory. She led a group called the Blossoms, who Spector recruited, in 1962, to sing “He’s a Rebel,” the track that became the prototype for the Wall of Sound. The song was supposed to have been sung by the Crystals, but they were 3,000 miles away in New York, and Spector, eager to rush the song into production, figured it didn’t matter — he could just credit the Crystals (which he did), and no one would know.
	

	Darlene Love sings “He’s a Rebel” with a saucy majesty that builds in power, until it becomes almost lordly in its reverence-for-the-bad-boy. (It’s no accident that Kenneth Anger, in “Scorpio Rising,” transposed the song so that she was singing about Jesus.) Her voice is as big as the Wall of Sound she helped to create. She sang lead on another Crystals track, “He’s Sure the Boy I Love,” did the background vocals on many other Spector songs — and, in 1963, sang “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” the greatest pop-music Christmas song ever recorded. She was credited on that one, but “The Phil Spector Christmas Album” had the misfortune to be released on Nov. 22, 1963, the day JFK was shot. The record fizzled; after a few weeks, Spector suppressed any further distribution of it. The album was essentially lost (until it was reissued by Apple Records in 1972). So even though Darlene Love had been billed on the album’s greatest track, her name remained lost as well.
	

	Thirteen years ago, Morgan Neville’s documentary “20 Feet from Stardom” paid tribute to rock ‘n’ roll’s most fabled back-up singers (the majority of whom were Black), and to how they spent their careers standing in the shadows. Darlene Love was one of those singers, and she featured prominently in the film; when it won the Oscar for best documentary, it was Love who stood up at the Academy Awards and gave an indelible speech. “20 Feet from Stardom” captured a very particular situation: The artists it was about didn’t get to be stars, but the movie suggested that in an alternate universe they might have been.

	Darlene Love, however, has lived a special, heightened version of that conundrum. She hovered in the background, not getting the recognition she deserved. At the same time, she was a star. Not a maximal one, but if being a true pop singer means singing lead on some of the most magical recordings of the 20th century, Love did that. She was out there in front, spearheading the sound. It was her name that was erased, so in a strange way her identity got erased too. You knew that voice in your sonic bones, but it was in front of you and invisible at the same time.

	Darlene Love didn’t need an alternate universe (she lived in both universes), and “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” tracks the unique fusion of glory, injustice, fleeting opportunity, dashed dreams, resilience, and latter-day recognition that defines her story. The movie, like Love’s life and career, is a one-of-a-kind ride, and by the end you don’t just feel like you know and understand this remarkable artist. You feel closer to the center of the mysteries of pop.

	Love is 85 now, but in the documentary, which is built around a present-day interview with her (though there’s also a ton of great archival footage), she’s ageless. Under a wig of orange-blonde curls, her face beams, her smile dances, her laugh rings out, her personality is funky and vivid, and she simply doesn’t seem old. Love got to know Paul Shaffer when David Letterman fell in love with “Christmas (Baby Please Don’t Come)” and decided, in 1986, to feature Love singing it on his late-night show (a performance that became an annual ritual). The documentary sets up Love with Shaffer leading a band in a studio of the Power Station, where she performs updated renditions of several of her key songs. Her voice is extraordinary, the force and quality of it undimmed. And Love proves a great narrator of her own legend. She knows what she was robbed of (not just credit but the life she could have had), yet she has transcended bitterness.
	

	The film’s director, Barry Avrich, takes us back to the age of radio (he pays nifty homage to it in the opening credits), when you would hear a voice coming out of that box, and the voice took hold of you. Love, born Darlene Wright in 1941, shuttled between Los Angeles and Texas and spent her first 15 years in church, dunked in gospel as much as Aretha or Ray Charles were. She joined the Blossoms in the late ’50s, and they sang backup on a host of classics, starting with Sam Cooke’s “Everybody Likes to Cha Cha Cha” and then on “Chain Gang” and “Rockin’ Robin,” “Monster Mash” and “Johnny Angel.”

	From there, they moved on to Phil Spector. They worked for him as back-up singers, in addition to being swapped in for the Crystals and Bob B. Soxx and the Blue Jeans, for whom Love sang lead on the sublimely lilting “Why Do Lovers Break Each Other’s Hearts.” Spector was a holy terror even then (though he was also a genius), and the name game he played with his female soul singers, moving them around as if they were interchangeable game-board pieces, was designed to do several things at once. It made Spector himself the star. (He was the first producer to do that.) It enabled him to withhold royalties. And in the largest sense, it was his (racist) way of treating all his talent like indentured servants.

	Love became a magnetic presence on “Shindig!,” the great rock ‘n’ roll TV show that allowed its performers to be wild and woolly (Shaffer offers a great reminiscence of it). She led the Blossoms in back-up vocals on pop songs from “Monday, Monday” to the Beach Boys’ “In My Room,” and she went on tour with the other Spector singers, falling into a serious relationship with Bill Medley of the Righteous Brothers. Onstage, she had a toothy insolence.

	Her career was a string of missed opportunities, including one that sounds like a conspiracy theory, though as presented in “I Know Where I’ve Been” it’s a fascinating one. Love was originally set to record “River Deep, Mountain High” for Phil Spector. At the last minute, he changed the singer to Tina Turner — and the song was, of course, a legendary commercial flop, the one that effectively ended Spector’s reign. The theory presented is that Turner’s rendition of it had too much R&B grit to succeed on the pop charts of 1966. Whereas Love, who had a much smoother pop-soul croon, would have made it a hit. Ah, the seduction of alternate-universe thinking! The documentary reveals how Spector became a creepier presence with the years and continued to shadow her, at one point buying out a contract she had with someone else. There’s no doubt that Spector’s great songs made her career, but the way he designed it they also nipped it in the bud.
	

	Love was still singing in the early ’70s (we hear her do a spellbinding rendition of “I’ll Be There”), but as the age of peak R&B wound down, so did her opportunities. She was married several times and had four children, two of whom got involved in the L.A. gang-banger scene and wound up in prison. (They have since emerged and triumphed.) Love wound up cleaning houses. Yet she was not forgotten. Bruce Springsteen and Steven Van Zandt, both fans from way back, took an interest in her (they are interviewed extensively). She wound up reviving her career by doing nostalgia-act performances on cruise ships. This ultimately led to the 1984 jukebox musical revue “Leader of the Pack,” which she was featured in as it began performances in the Greenwich Village club the Bottom Line; it became a sensation. The documentary hints that it was also successful when it moved to Broadway (which isn’t the case; it flamed out there), but Darlene Love was relaunched.

	And as much as that, she was recognized. The exultant Letterman performances of “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” featuring bigger choirs each year, helped a great deal, and so did her 2011 induction into the Rock ‘n’ Roll Hall of Fame. Suddenly, everyone knew who Darlene Love was. “I Know Where I’ve Been” completes the journey. It’s a film that leaves you staggered — at the soul-stirring splendor of her voice, at the forces of the time, both big and small, that marginalized her, and at our awareness of what might have been, which should never stand in the way of our awe at what was.

schema.headline: ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name

title: Paramount and California AG Bonta Reportedly in ‘Advanced Talks’ to Settle Antitrust Suit
description: David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance is in “advanced talks” with California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle the 12-state antitrust suit that’s ho
body:
David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance is in “advanced talks” with California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle the 12-state antitrust suit that’s holding up its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing anonymous sources. 

	A Paramount spokesperson declined to comment. A rep for Bonta’s office said, “Potential settlement talks are confidential. We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.”
	

	Per the Journal’s report, the talks are “ongoing and there is no guarantee that an agreement will be reached.” Paramount and the California AG have “discussed compromises including Paramount agreeing to operate the two companies’ movie studios separately for a period rather than immediately combining them,” according to the WSJ article.


	However, Bonta has previously said that running the two companies separately — but under common ownership — would be a mere “behavioral” remedy, and that he is looking for a structural remedy that would entail separate ownership.

	RELATED STORY: Who is Rob Bonta and Why is California’s Attorney General Suing to Block Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger?

	A judge has scheduled a trial in the matter for March 2027. Paramount had requested that the 12 states — and the Writers Guild of America, which also has filed an antitrust suit seeking to block the Paramount-WBD deal — post a $1.88 billion bond to cover its potential losses from a “ticking fee” payable to WBD shareholders (starting as of Oct. 1 at a rate of $7 million per day) if Paramount ends up prevailing in court. A hearing on the bond motion is set for Sept. 24.
	

	Ellison’s $111 billion pending deal for Warner Bros. Discovery is being bankrolled in part by his mega-billionaire father, Larry Ellison, as well as the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. On Thursday, the FCC approved Paramount’s petition to allow 49.5% of its equity to be held by foreign entities if the Warner Bros. Discovery is consummated.

	David Ellison has internally told Paramount execs he’s seriously considering relocating the company’s operations — including, over a longer time horizon, its studio — out of California if Paramount is unable to close the Warner Bros. deal by the end of September. He’s floated the possibility of moving the company to Tennessee, Texas or Georgia.

schema.headline: Paramount and California AG Bonta Reportedly in ‘Advanced Talks’ to Settle Antitrust Suit

title: Angelina Jolie and Salma Hayek Pinault on Their New Film ‘Without Blood’ and Spending ‘A Lot of Time Talking About Our Pain, Our Losses, Our Traumas’
description: In “Without Blood,” written and directed by Angelina Jolie, Salma Hayek plays Nina, a woman who spends her adult life looking for the three men resp
body:
In “Without Blood,” written and directed by Angelina Jolie, Salma Hayek plays Nina, a woman who spends her adult life looking for the three men responsible for the wartime murder of her father and brother when she was just a child.

	In two of the cases, her revenge is fatal. But then she meets the third accomplice, Tito (Demián Bichir), now a clerk in a newspaper kiosk at a train station.


	The movie is in many ways a two-hander featuring Nina and Tito talking over drinks with flashback scenes chronicling both of their sometimes harrowing lives.
	

	“I was afraid that I couldn’t play this part, and also I was afraid to go so far every day at work and go into this really difficult place,” Hayek says during a joint interview with Jolie. “At the beginning, I wasn’t sure that Angelina was directing. I thought she was just producing. I’m like, ‘Oh no, I don’t want to suffer like that. I don’t want to.’ And then she started talking to me about the importance of the piece. And then you have to understand that Angelina is an extraordinary director.”




	

					Salma Hayek Pinault stars in “Without Blood.”
									Courtesy Image
	



	“Without Blood” is an adaptation of Italian writer Alessandro Baricco’s novella of the same name. Like the book, the movie doesn’t specify the time or the location where the story takes place, nor identify the war at the center of the story. The characters speak English and Spanish.

	“I wanted it to be that anyone watching it from anywhere could identify with it,” Jolie says. “Even if it wasn’t an actual war or a conflict, there’s something beautiful in the book where it says, ‘We return to where we break.’ So part of the conflict and the idea of the film is that anybody can identify with something in your life where something happened where it broke you and changed you, and how much you wish you could sit across from that person and have answers and have some kind of say your piece and hope that they could see you and hope that it gives you some kind of healing or closure. Of course, sometimes it doesn’t give you what you think you’re looking for or doesn’t heal those.” 
	

	This isn’t the first time Jolie has made a film about war and conflict. Her directorial debut was the Bosnian war drama “In the Land of Blood and Money” in 2011. “Unbroken” (2014) told the story of American prisoners-of-war during World War II. The life of Cambodian author and human rights activist Loung Ung under the rule of the Khmer Rouge was the subject of “First They Killed My Father” in 2017.

	“In ‘First They Killed My Father,’ we had trauma therapy tents because a lot of people there had been through war and I’ve learned that everybody’s been through some level of trauma,” Jolie says. “What we did on this was the time spent with everybody discussing it. We all ended up spending a lot of time talking about our pain, talking about our losses, our traumas. Obviously, community can be very, very healing.”

	Jolie and Hayek Pinault first worked together five years ago when they co-starred in the Marvel movie “Eternals.” Next, Jolie will serve as a producer on Hayek Pinault’s directorial debut, “Arena,” an epic romantic adventure that the “Frida” star also wrote.

	“In a way, she’s my partner,” Hayek Pinault says. “I’ve written two different scripts with two different pens that she gave me. It’s a really good, enriching and artistic relationship. That is hard to find. It’s such a gift.”

	I asked Jolie if she’s ever been tempted to direct lighter material like a comedy. “We’ve laughed a lot. We fantasized about making different comedies together,” Hayek Pinault says.

	Jolie laughs, “My comedies tend to be a bit dark. I think I have a dark sense of humor.”

	Hayek Pinault turns to Jolie and says, “You’re funny. So funny. She just keeps it a secret.”

	Jolie isn’t sure she has what it takes to helm comedy. “I don’t know how good I’d be. You have those things that we think, as an actress, you like to try everything and then you get to a point you realize other actors are good at certain things and there are many who are better at comedy than I am. But I do think I’m a pretty good straight person, like the ‘Maleficent.’ I’m a good straight.”

	“Without Blood” is in theaters now.

schema.headline: Angelina Jolie and Salma Hayek Pinault on Their New Film ‘Without Blood’ and Spending ‘A Lot of Time Talking About Our Pain, Our Losses, Our Traumas’

title: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Canceled at Netflix as Sheryl J. Anderson and JoAnna Garcia Swisher Set New Series ‘Ladies of the House’
description:
It’s bittersweet news for “Sweet Magnolias.”

	The romantic drama starring JoAnna Garcia Swisher, Brooke Elliott and Heather Headley has been cancel
body:
It’s bittersweet news for “Sweet Magnolias.”

	The romantic drama starring JoAnna Garcia Swisher, Brooke Elliott and Heather Headley has been canceled at Netflix after five seasons. But Swisher, alongside “Sweet Magnolias” creator Sheryl J. Anderson, are pairing up for a new drama series ordered by the streamer titled “Ladies of the House.”

	Anderson will serve as showrunner of “Ladies of the House,” with Swisher potentially starring and executive producing with Kate Gordon under their Rolling Clover banner, alongside executive producers at Black Label Media. The show is loosely based on the novel by Lauren Edmonson.
	

	The logline reads, “When the charismatic owner of a winery dies unexpectedly, his wife and two adult daughters must battle through their issues with each other in order to confront challenges with the business, their extended family, and the men in their lives. Good friends and good wine will aid in the journey to hang on to the winery, but what matters most is that they find a way to hang on to each other.”


	“I’m thrilled to be embarking on this new adventure with JoAnna and Netflix,” said Anderson. “When Jo shared the novel with me, I immediately saw the foundation for a series centered on three women grappling with the complexities of family, friendship, and romance — the kind of stories Jo and I most enjoy telling. I cannot wait to share the Richardson women and their world with Netflix’s global audience.”

	Swisher added, “From the moment I read Lauren Edmondson’s Ladies of the House, I fell completely in love with Daisy, Cricket and Wallis: their relationships, their messiness, their strength, and most of all, their heart. I am beyond excited to continue to tell meaningful, female-driven stories alongside the incredible Sheryl J. Anderson, and to bring this to life through our production company Rolling Clover and with our wonderful partners at Black Label. Netflix has been my creative home for the past seven years, and I couldn’t imagine a better place, or a better team, to tell this story.”
	

	Deadline broke the news.

schema.headline: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Canceled at Netflix as Sheryl J. Anderson and JoAnna Garcia Swisher Set New Series ‘Ladies of the House’

title: ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Proves the Show Just Wouldn’t Work Without Tom Hardy
description: A mere 10 minutes into the Season 2 premiere of “MobLand,” aptly titled “I Wanna Be Your Dog,” there is a massacre at the racetrack. Increasingly on
body: A mere 10 minutes into the Season 2 premiere of “MobLand,” aptly titled “I Wanna Be Your Dog,” there is a massacre at the racetrack. Increasingly on edge and triggered by his son Kevin’s (Paddy Considine) disloyalty, Conrad Harrigan (Pierce Brosnan), patriarch of the Harrigan crime family, lets his temper get the best of him. In a spray of bullets, he ends an already tense partnership with the Turkish mob. Unmoved by the consequences of his own chaos, Conrad does what he’s done for years: call his longtime fixer, Harry Da Souza (Tom Hardy), to clean up his mess.​Erasing crime scenes, tying up loose ends and identifying threats is something Harry can do in his sleep. With a menacing calm that pulsates off of him, Harry is neither alarmed nor surprised when he receives a call from Conrad. But Harry’s position in the Harrigan dynasty has cost him a great deal. His 18-year marriage to his long-suffering wife Jan (Joanne Froggatt) is in trouble. (In fact, Harry is just now on the mend after accidentally being stabbed by Jan a couple of months prior.) Moreover, the couple’s teenage daughter, Gina (Teddie Allen), infuriated with her parents’ dysfunction, has run off with Kevin’s wannabe gangster son, Eddie (Anson Boon). Unfortunately, Harry doesn’t have the bandwidth to deal with his wife and daughter, and as usual he turns his attention to the Harrigans, whose family unit is coming apart at the seams. Even matriarch Maeve (Helen Mirren) seems intent on sabotaging her husband for her own gain or perhaps revenge for some festering resentment.  ​As the anchor in the “MobLand” universe, when reports began stirring earlier this spring that Hardy had been axed from the series, audiences were puzzled. The show centers around the work Harry executes to keep the Harrigans thriving in London’s criminal underworld while staying off law enforcement’s radar. Back then, Variety confirmed that after Season 2 wrapped this past March, Hardy fell out with executive producer Jez Butterworth, 101 Studios and others. At the time, reports said the clash was so severe that Hardy would not return for a third season.​The news of Hardy’s ousting ricocheted across the entertainment world, baffling fans and even some of Hardy’s “MobLand” co-stars. “Tom is a very special person,” Mirren told Variety at the Taormina Film Festival. “I think he’s absolutely remarkable. My support of him is genuine and heartfelt.” As the news spread, “MobLand” producers set a meeting with Hardy in London to hash things out. Now, he is officially returning for Season 3 of the Paramount+ series.​Though critics received just four episodes of the 10-episode second season of “MobLand” for review, what’s clear to any viewer is that Harry’s position within the Harrigan crime family is undergoing a major transformation. Growing increasingly weary of Conrad’s lack of impulse control, frustrated by Kevin’s cowardice and with his own personal life in shambles, Harry is undoubtedly coming closer to his boiling point.​After all, not only does he know where all the bodies are buried, but Harry moves with such a calculated callousness that he could very likely dismantle all Conrad and Maeve have built from the inside out. Since Hardy is returning for the third season of the show, Harry will be forced to choose a side, either standing firmly with the Harrigans or going his own way. For the Harrigans’ sake, let’s hope he remains an ally. If the Harrigans’ choose to make an enemy of Harry, what he could unleash would be more brutally murderous than anything Maeve or Conrad could begin to conjure.

schema.headline: ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Proves the Show Just Wouldn’t Work Without Tom Hardy

title: ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization
description: There’s nothing more distressing in “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ than the unflinching closeups of the author’s wounded body in th
body:
There’s nothing more distressing in “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ than the unflinching closeups of the author’s wounded body in the days and weeks after August 12, 2022, when he was repeatedly stabbed while on stage at a literary festival in upstate New York. The camera lingers over his mangled hand and the train-track of stitches running up his belly. His right eye is a bloodied bulge. The power of Alex Gibney’s documentary, which premiered at Sundance, lies in Rushdie’s decision to showcase his scars — quite literally, by sharing footage that his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths shot throughout his time in the hospital. It’s a visceral complement to what is otherwise a solid, if standard, profile of the author from Gibney, the Oscar- and Emmy-winner known for churning out reliably comprehensive, reporter-style investigations of power and politics.
	

	In Gibney’s upcoming “Musk,” an HBO-produced Elon Musk mega-doc that showed at Venice, the SpaceX and Tesla overlord is an AI-generated talking head. Thankfully no such uncanny simulations are in play here. The Indian-born writer has control of the mic from the get-go with running voiceover narration that starts the film alongside a feverish recreation of the attack visualized from Rushdie’s point of view: Blinding stage lights turn his assailant, a New Jersey man by the name of Hadi Matar, into a shadowy mass, and each jab of the knife is heard as a fleshy thud. Matar is only mentioned by name once. In Rushdie’s retelling, he becomes a symbol for the punishing incursions upon his life and liberties since the publication of his 1988 novel “The Satanic Verses” scandalized the masses and put a target on his head, courtesy of a fatwa issued by Ayatollah Khomeini, then the Supreme ruler of Iran.
	

	Wondering why he didn’t fight back or run away, Rushdie moves into an extended reflection on his relationship to death and fatalism. In the present thread, we follow his recovery through Griffiths’ tenderly diaristic documentation, which includes, at one point, a call from family friend Wes Anderson. Meanwhile Gibney employs archival news footage and old on-camera interviews with Rushdie to take us back to his identity-crisis-riddled early years between India and his adopted home of London, and the emotional abuse he suffered while living with his alcoholic father. But for the most part, Gibney keeps to the events after 1988, when Rushdie’s Islam-inspired magical realist tome became the flashpoint for a fiery debate over free speech and creative freedom.

	Excerpts from the novel are accompanied by scratchy animated renderings of the story — about two Indian-Muslim men living in London who undergo spiritual upheavals after surviving a plane crash — that echo Rushdie’s existential musings and emphasize the work as a product of his imagination. It’s a way of highlighting the absurdity of the violent response from orthodox Muslim communities —  all this rage for a story? — and more generally, the dangers that religious extremism poses to civil society. When Ayatollah Khomeini called for Rushdie’s righteous assassination in 1989, protests and book burnings broke out in the U.K., Pakistan and India; elsewhere, bookstores were destroyed, editorial offices torched, and Rushdie’s Japanese translator, Hitoshi Agarashi, was murdered. These aren’t breaking revelations for what is — for a certain generation, at least — one of the late 20th century’s most shocking and widely-discussed controversies.

	But lest we dismiss these events as contained to the past, the 2022 assault stands as a reminder that artistic expression remains as frighteningly vulnerable as Rushdie’s brutalized body. That message might feel obvious for anyone even remotely tapped into the American news cycle, but it’s given a weighty (if obligatorily sentimental) personal touch by the resilient Rushdie and his support system, led by the tenacious Griffiths — his rock against a seemingly neverending saga.

schema.headline: ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization

title: Dana Walden Envisions Partnerships Between Creators and Disney at Created in L.A. Kickoff Event: ‘Maybe We Can Tell Some Stories Together’

body:
Disney kicked off its first creator event Created in L.A on Thursday night at El Capitan Theatre in Hollywood.

	Over 350 creators, innovators and industry leaders came together for the first day of a two-day event with the idea to exchange ideas, build relationships, and explore the future of creator-led storytelling and the business behind it.

	Opening the evening was creator, entrepreneur and media personality Jon Youshaei. The event was conceived and hosted by Youshaei, whose career involves leadership roles at YouTube and Instagram, as well as his own success as a creator. He is known for in-depth interviews and behind-the-scenes conversations with creators and entertainers including MrBeast, Mark Rober and Kevin Hart.
	

	Youshaei highlighted the power of the creators in the room, many of whom had traveled from Argentina, Australia, England, Netherlands, Canada, Georgia and Morocco to attend. He also highlighted their social media followings: “The creators at this event have over 800 million subscribers on YouTube, 80 million followers on Instagram and over 350 million followers on TikTok, which altogether makes over 1.6 billion followers combined.”


	After sharing a brief history of the theater, Youshaei recounted his pitch to Disney about showcasing the work of creators. He told the audience, “I said, ‘Hey, I have this crazy idea. What if we premiere videos from creators on the big screen? I’m talking about the same videos we usually watch on our phones and our laptops, but have recently gotten so damn good that they deserve to be played in a theater, that deserve to be premiered on a red carpet, that deserve to be celebrated with 350 of the most creative people in the world?’”
	

	The executives at Disney said yes, resulting in the creation of this two-day event, which also includes keynote speakers and conversations.

	Dana Walden, president and chief creative officer of the Walt Disney Company, noted how special the theater i s for Disney, having hosted the premieres of iconic films such as “The Lion King,” “The Avengers,” “Frozen,” “Coco” and “Lilo & Stitch.”

	She also acknowledged the vital role creators play in Disney’s ecosystem.

	“What strikes me about this room is the instinct so many of you have for your audience. You know them intimately. You hear from them constantly, and you adjust in real time based on what they want. And that is very different from the kind of content that we produce.” She elaborated, “It can take years for our films and series to reach their audiences and for you it could be seconds. And there’s something that we can learn from that immediacy, from treating the audience as a true collaborator. My hope for these two days is that we’ll exchange ideas and learn from each other — that some of what makes your storytelling so special rubs off on us, and that some of what we’ve learned about telling stories over many decades will be useful to you.”

	Walden concluded by expressing her hope that Created in L.A. would herald the beginning of incredible relationships. “Maybe we can tell some stories together.”

	The evening concluded with Youshaei introducing the Golden State Award. The award recognizes strong filmmakers or subscriber count. 

	The first award went to Lucas and Curtis Nicotra, who go by the name Sticks. Their film “The Technoblade Movie,” premiered alongside Zach King’s parody of “Star Wars,” “Cardboard Strikes Back.” King received the second Golden State Award.

title: Sesame Street Transforms Chappell Roan’s ‘Hot to Go!’ Into the Potty-Training Anthem ‘Got to Go,’ With Lead Vocals From Cookie Monster
description: Sesame Street has a half-century-long tradition of legendary musical guests and innovative adaptations: from Stevie Wonder’s iconic performance in t
body:
Sesame Street has a half-century-long tradition of legendary musical guests and innovative adaptations: from Stevie Wonder’s iconic performance in the early ‘70s to Tony Bennett retrofitting his timeless classic “Fly Me to the Moon” to be a story about the show’s worm character Slimy on an expedition to the moon (“Slimy to the Moon,” of course); from the Fugees’ inclusion anthem “Just Happy to Be Me” to blues legend B.B. King singing an ode to the letter that has meant so much to his career; from Smokey Robinson getting groped by the letter “U” for “U Really Got a Hold on Me” to — this writer’s personal favorite — opera legend Marilyn Horne trilling an orchestral version of “C Is for Cookie” on an elaborate mock-Egyptian set while wearing a tiara adorned with a bouncing cookie.
	

	And some 57 years after the show premiered, its brilliant combination of education, musicality and humor continues: In a newly released video, they transform Chappell Roan’s “Hot to Go” into a potty-training anthem called “Got to Go” with inimitable lead vocals from the Cookie Monster.




	It’s a note-for-note rendition too, complete with the song’s chanted middle section from guest vocalists Elmo and Abby Cadabby, and even some toilet-flushing sound effects. And although we don’t get to see Muppets doing the world-famous hand-gestures spelling out the song’s title, instead we get singing letters spelling out POTTY.

	Cookie Monster intones in his trademark broken English:

	“Stop and listen to me body/ It’s saying that it’s time for potty,There’s a growing feeling in my tummy, that me gotta go pee, me gotta go pee…There they go again, now me legs are grooving/ There might be a mess if me don’t get movin’…
	

	“P-O-T-T-Y, woah-oh, your body knows when you’ve got to go…”

	It even starts with a talking number one and two. 

	Contacted by Variety, a rep for Chappell Roan said the singer had no comment. Indeed, none was necessary: Granting permission for her and cowriter/producer Dan Nigro’s song to be used in such an amusing and imaginatively instructive way — for young children, no less — is a statement in itself.

schema.headline: Sesame Street Transforms Chappell Roan’s ‘Hot to Go!’ Into the Potty-Training Anthem ‘Got to Go,’ With Lead Vocals From Cookie Monster

title: Ed Sheeran Ready to Perform Philadelphia Show Solo If Needed Amid Macklemore Exit
description:
Ed Sheeran
                          No Issue Being One Man Band
body:
Ed Sheeran
                          No Issue Being One Man Band
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 18, 2026
                            6:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ed Sheeran is ready to perform Saturday night's Philadelphia concert solo if needed, now that Macklemore, the rest of his openers and his backup band are out ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Music industry sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... plans for the concert have been changing hour by hour behind the scenes as everyone works out the logistics. But we're told there's no concern about Ed taking the stage by himself if it comes to that.
      
    
            Our sources point out Ed has historically performed in large-scale venues with nothing more than a guitar ... and has successfully carried two-hour stadium shows without a backup band.
      

            We're told that makes the current situation different from what it would be for other artists ... because Ed is the headliner and the tour's primary ticket seller as it is.
      
    
            The good news for Ed and his fans ... our sources note Ed is the kind of artist who can walk onto a stage with a guitar and perform for two hours by himself without missing a beat.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Macklemore was removed from the tour after his pro-Palestine remarks sparked major backlash. The fallout continued with opening act Aaron Rowe, Finneas, and Ed's band Beoga backing out while voicing support for Palestinians.
      
    
            Macklemore later pledged to donate the $1 million he earned on Ed's "Loop" Tour to Palestinian relief groups and challenged New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft to match it. Kraft went even further ... pledging $2 million.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Macklemore has claimed pressure from NFL team owners, including Kraft, led to his removal. The owners run the stadiums where Ed's scheduled to perform ... including Philly.
      
    
            Ed, meanwhile, has said his hands were tied.

title: 'Love & Hip Hop' Star D. Smith Detransitioning After 12 Years Living As a Woman
description:
'Love & Hip Hop' Star D. Smith
                          Ending 12-Year Life as a Trans Woman
body:
'Love & Hip Hop' Star D. Smith
                          Ending 12-Year Life as a Trans Woman
                          ... Has No Regrets
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 18, 2026
                            5:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            "Love & Hip Hop: Atlanta" alum D. Smith says he's detransitioning after living publicly as a transgender woman for 12 years ... and will now present as a man and use he/him pronouns.
      
    
            The Grammy-nominated producer announced the change Thursday on Instagram, saying the decision has been taking shape over the past several months.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Smith says those years were not a mistake and aren't something he's trying to erase ... writing, "Living my life as a woman for 12 years showed me the man that I wanted to become."
      

            He also stressed his love and respect for the transgender community remain unchanged ... and says everyone deserves the freedom to become themselves.
      
    
            Smith added there's much more to his journey than he could fit into one statement, and plans to share the full story when the time is right.
      
    
            He publicly came out as transgender in 2014 and joined "Love & Hip Hop: Atlanta" two years later ... becoming the show's first openly transgender cast member.
      
    
            The two-time Grammy nominee has worked on music with artists including Katy Perry, Lil Wayne, and CeeLo Green.

title: Frankie Muniz's Estranged Wife Shares Cryptic Message After He Says He’s Hit 'Rock Bottom'
description:
Frankie Muniz's Estranged Wife
                          Gets Cryptic After His 'Rock Bottom' Adm
body:
Frankie Muniz's Estranged Wife
                          Gets Cryptic After His 'Rock Bottom' Admission
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Frankie Muniz's estranged wife, Paige Price, shared a cryptic message about perspective shortly after the actor revealed he's been going through an intensely difficult period.
      
    
            Price posted an Instagram Story Friday featuring a video of herself making a wax seal ... writing, "Life is all about perspective. If you ask the grass, the zebra is the monster and the lion is the protector."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The clip was set to an acoustic version of the Goo Goo Dolls' "Iris," including lyrics about not wanting the world to see or understand you.
      

            Price's post came just hours after Muniz opened up about his recent struggles on Instagram.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            "The last 6 weeks of my life have been a nightmare I'm praying to wake up from," the "Malcolm in the Middle" star wrote. "Everything has felt heavy, unclear, and like it has been falling apart at the same time."
      
    
            Muniz said he’s been forced to confront parts of himself he wants to change ... describing the experience as an "unexpected gift." He also acknowledged hitting "rock bottom," but said he believes the low point will eventually serve as the foundation for a better future.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The actor ended his message by encouraging anyone else in a difficult place ... writing they're "not broken" but "being rebuilt."
      
    
            Muniz and Price announced in July they were ending their marriage after 10 years together. The estranged couple, who share 5-year-old son Mauz, said they planned to remain friends and co-parents.
      
    
            Price previously defended Muniz after backlash over his original divorce announcement ... insisting they were still "on the same team."
